title: Faraday’s Law of Induction: Lenz’s Law
lead: A change in the magnetic flux through a coil drives an emf, and Faraday’s experiments settled exactly what that emf depends on: how much the flux changes, how quickly it changes, and how many turns of wire the change passes through. This section states Faraday’s law of induction, explains the minus sign in front of it as Lenz’s law, which says that the induced current always opposes the change that produced it, gives the six steps for finding the direction of an induced current, and ends with the recording heads, hard drives, cochlear implants and breathing monitors that induction is already at work in.
objectives: Calculate emf, current, and magnetic fields using Faraday’s Law.
Explain the physical results of Lenz’s Law
summary_html:
• Faraday’s law of induction states that the emf induced by a change in magnetic flux is $\kemf = -N\frac{\kdPhi}{\kdt}$ when flux changes by $\kdPhi$ in a time $\kdt$.
  • If emf is induced in a coil, $N$ is its number of turns.
  • The minus sign means that the emf creates a current $\kIcur$ and magnetic field $\kBmag$ that oppose the change in flux $\kdPhi$—this opposition is known as Lenz’s law.

exercises.prompt: A person who works with large magnets sometimes places her head inside a strong field. She reports feeling dizzy as she quickly turns her head. How might this be associated with induction?

answer.solution: Turning her head quickly changes the orientation of everything inside it with respect to the field, and by $\kPhi = \kBmag A\cos\theta$ a change in orientation is a change in flux. Any closed conducting path in the head, and the fluid and tissue of the head is conducting, then has a changing flux through it, so by Faraday’s law an emf is induced round that path and a small current flows. The faster she turns, the smaller $\kdt$ is and the larger the induced emf, which is why the dizziness comes with a quick turn and not with a slow one. Currents induced in the fluid of the inner ear and in the nerves that report the position of the head are enough to be felt as dizziness, and nothing is induced at all while she holds her head still, however strong the field is.

exercises.prompt: A particle accelerator sends high-velocity charged particles down an evacuated pipe. Could a coil of wire wrapped around the pipe detect the passage of individual particles via an induced emf? If so, sketch a graph of the voltage output of the coil as a single particle passes through it. If not, determine what orientation of the coil would allow detection of the particle and explain why this orientation is needed.

answer.solution: It could. A moving charge carries a magnetic field of its own, which circles the line of its motion by RHR-2, and a coil wound around the pipe has its own axis along that line. As the particle comes up to the coil the flux of its field through the coil rises, and as it goes away again the flux falls, so the coil sees a flux that rises and then falls and Faraday’s law gives an emf throughout. The graph of the output against time is a pulse one way followed by a pulse the other way, crossing zero at the moment the particle is in the plane of the coil, because that is the moment when the flux is at its largest and is momentarily not changing. The pulse is short and its height grows with the speed of the particle, since a faster particle makes the same change of flux in a smaller $\kdt$. Whether a single particle can be detected in practice is a question of how large that emf is beside the noise of the amplifier; the emf of one particle is very small, which is why real accelerators read a bunch of many particles at once rather than one.

exercises.prompt: (a) An MRI technician moves his hand from a region of very low magnetic field strength into an MRI scanner’s 2.00 T field with his fingers pointing in the direction of the field. Find the average emf induced in his wedding ring, given its diameter is 2.20 cm and assuming it takes 0.250 s to move it into the field. (b) Discuss whether this current would significantly change the temperature of the ring.

answer.hint: The ring starts where the field is almost nothing and ends in a 2.00 T field with its face square to it, so the flux through it goes from nearly zero to $\kBmag A$. Work out the area from the diameter and divide the change in flux by the time; the ring is a single turn, so $N = 1$.
answer.solution: (a) 3.04 mV (b) As a lower limit on the ring, estimate R = 1.00 mΩ. The heat transferred will be 2.31 mJ. This is not a significant amount of heat.

exercises.prompt: An emf is induced by rotating a 1000-turn, 20.0 cm diameter coil in the Earth’s $5.00\times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ magnetic field. What average emf is induced, given the plane of the coil is originally perpendicular to the Earth’s field and is rotated to be parallel to the field in 10.0 ms?

answer.hint: The coil begins with its plane perpendicular to the field, so the flux through it is $\kBmag A$, and ends with its plane parallel to the field, where the flux is zero. The whole of that flux is therefore lost in 10.0 ms, and each of the 1000 turns contributes its own emf.
